questions.stem: A team turns on a preview feature in its Maven build with `--enable-preview --release 21`, and its tests, run by the build with the same flag, pass. The service is then started on Java 21 with `java -jar billing.jar` and no other options. What happens?

options.text: It starts and runs normally, since the compiler already enabled the feature inside the class files it wrote
options.says: the compiler only marks the class file (minor version 65535); the JVM refuses a marked class unless it is started with --enable-preview

options.text: It starts and runs until the feature's code is first executed, since the JVM checks a preview feature when the code that uses it runs
options.says: the check is made on the class file's version when the class loads, before any of its code runs

options.text: It fails when the first marked class loads, since the JVM accepts such classes only when it was started with the flag too
options.says: java without --enable-preview throws UnsupportedClassVersionError: Preview features are not enabled ... (class file version 65.65535)

options.text: It fails when the jar is opened, since a jar holding such classes must declare the flag in its manifest
options.says: the failure is a LinkageError on loading the marked class, and the fix is --enable-preview on the java command

origin.section: Preview Features Must Be Switched On Twice, at Compile Time and at Run Time

questions.stem: A shared library was compiled with `--enable-preview --release 22` because one class uses a feature that was in preview in 22. The services that use it move to Java 23 and keep `--enable-preview` on their `java` command. What happens when that class is loaded on 23?

options.text: It loads, since a class compiled for one release loads on every later release that is started with the flags it needs
options.says: that holds for ordinary classes only; a class marked as using previews loads only on the release that compiled it

options.text: It loads, since a later release accepts the previews of earlier releases and reports any that have changed
options.says: the later JVM refuses the class outright: it only recognizes preview features for its own class file version

options.text: It is refused, since a class that uses preview features loads only on the release that compiled it
options.says: Java 25 refused a 65.65535 class: it only recognizes preview features for class file version 69.65535

options.text: It is refused, since a class compiled for one release loads only on a runtime of exactly that release
options.says: an ordinary class loads on its release and every later one; only preview classes are tied to one release

origin.section: A Preview Class File Runs Only on the Release That Compiled It

questions.stem: A reporting tool moves from Java 11 to Java 17 with no new dependencies. At startup it stores `new ScriptEngineManager().getEngineByName("JavaScript")` in a field; the engine is used only when a user exports a report that contains formulas. What does the team see?

options.text: The tool fails at startup, since the lookup throws an exception when no engine has that name
options.says: getEngineByName returns null for an unknown name; it throws only when the name is null

options.text: The tool fails at startup, since the JDK's script engine classes it was compiled against are gone
options.says: javax.script is still in the JDK; only the Nashorn engine was removed, so the lookup finds nothing

options.text: The tool starts, and the first export with formulas fails with a NullPointerException, since the lookup returned null
options.says: with Nashorn removed the lookup returns null, and the failure appears where the engine is first used

options.text: The tool starts, and the first export with formulas fails with a ScriptException, since the lookup returned an engine that runs no language
options.says: there is no placeholder engine: on 21 the JDK lists no script engines at all and the lookup returns null

origin.section: Nashorn Is Gone, and the Engine Lookup Returns null Instead of Failing

questions.stem: A service on a new JVM prints two warnings at startup and then runs. One option, `-XX:+A`, was deprecated in an earlier release; the other, `-XX:+B`, became obsolete in this release. Which of the two still change how the running JVM behaves?

options.text: Both of them, since the JVM warns about an option for a release or two before it stops applying it
options.says: an obsolete option is accepted and ignored; only the deprecated one still works

options.text: Neither of them, since the JVM stops applying an option in the same release that it starts warning about it
options.says: a deprecated option still works and warns; only an obsolete one is ignored

options.text: Only `-XX:+A`, since the JVM keeps applying a deprecated option and only accepts and skips an obsolete one
options.says: deprecated: works and warns; obsolete: accepted, ignored, with a warning

options.text: Only `-XX:+B`, since the JVM keeps applying an obsolete option and only accepts and skips a deprecated one
options.says: an obsolete option is ignored, and a deprecated one still works

origin.section: A Removed JVM Option Is Ignored for a While, Then Stops the JVM From Starting
